did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah begins his prophecy about Tyre by calling on the ships of Tarshish to wail, because Tyre’s harbor and maritime trade had been devastated.
Did you know? Tyre is described as a commercial center sustained by Egypt’s grain: the produce of the Nile was carried to it by sea, and it became a merchant for many nations.
Did you know? The sea itself is portrayed as being ashamed of Tyre and mourning for her—a vivid expression emphasizing the magnitude of her downfall and the damage to her maritime standing.
Did you know? Tyre is called a crowned city, and its merchants are described as princes and the honored people of the land—evidence of its wealth, influence, and central role in international trade.

Did you know? According to the prophecy, it is the Lord who determined to humble Tyre’s pride and bring down the status of the honored people of the land; thus, the city’s destruction is presented as part of divine judgment.

Did you know? The people of Tyre are told to cross over to the land of Kittim, but even there they will find no rest. Thus, the prophecy emphasizes not only the loss of the city but also the wandering of its inhabitants.

Did you know? The land of the Chaldeans is presented in the prophecy as a power that brings destruction on fortified cities. The verse connects the rise of the Chaldeans with turning palaces and strongholds into ruins.

Did you know? Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, a period compared with the days of one king. Afterward, it will return to its activities, but its portrayal as a prostitute is a mocking expression for its commercial exploitation.

Did you know? In the conclusion of the prophecy, Tyre’s merchandise is not stored up for itself but becomes holy to the Lord and serves as food and clothing for those who dwell in his presence. Thus, its commercial wealth is given a new purpose.
